# Testing

- TST-004: Coverage gates: 100% line coverage for pure domain assemblies, 95% for application assemblies, 90% overall; mutation score 85% (nightly).
- TST-010: A test's name should consist of three parts, the name of the method being tested, the scenario under which it's tested, and the expected behavior when the scenario is invoked. Try to include only one Act task per test. Avoid manual string concatenation and logical conditions (if, while, for, switch) in unit tests, and avoid magic strings: assign hard-coded values to constants. A unit test's input should be the simplest information needed to verify the behavior under test. Try not to introduce dependencies on infrastructure into unit tests; they should be reserved for integration tests. To keep test-specific setup visible, create the objects a test needs in the test or call a helper method from it, in preference to Setup and Teardown attributes when tests have different setup requirements; common per-test setup can still be appropriate when every test in a class needs the same initialization, and for synchronous initialization, prefer the constructor. In most cases you don't need to test a private method: write the tests against the public method that calls it. A unit test must have full control of the system under test, so where production code calls static references (for example, DateTime.Now), you need to introduce a seam into the production code.
- TST-011: The kit's additions to its unit tests, beyond Microsoft's best practices (TST-010): write each test name as the method, the scenario and the expected behavior without underscores (AddRejectsAMissingRequestByName); arrange, act and assert; keep try out of a test; shared setup is a helper method, not a constructor every test runs (this departs from TST-010's "for synchronous initialization, prefer the constructor": the kit's tests don't); and bring time, randomness and other outside state in through seams such as TimeProvider.
- TST-012: Avoid ordering unit tests: it's best practice, and ideally the order in which they run should not matter.
